definition: Molecule mining is the process of data mining, or extracting and discovering patterns, as applied to molecules.
details: Since molecules may be represented by molecular graphs, this is strongly related to graph mining and structured data mining. The main problem is how to represent molecules while discriminating the data instances. One way to do this is chemical similarity metrics, which has a long tradition in the field of cheminformatics. Typical approaches to calculate chemical similarities use chemical fingerprints, but this loses the underlying information about the molecule topology. Mining the molecular graphs directly avoids this problem. So does the inverse QSAR problem which is preferable for vectorial mappings.

explainer.lead: Molecule mining applies data mining to molecules to extract and discover patterns. It matters because molecular data is structured, so how molecules are represented shapes what patterns can be found.

tiers.eli5: Like sorting a huge collection of keys by their shape to find which ones open similar locks.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers treat molecules as molecular graphs and mine the graph structure, drawing on graph and structured data mining. A pitfall is relying only on chemical fingerprints for similarity: that works but loses the underlying information about molecule topology.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, it is data mining applied to molecules represented as molecular graphs, closely related to graph and structured data mining, with the central problem being representation that discriminates data instances; chemical similarity via fingerprints discards topology.

explainer.example: Instead of comparing molecules only by fingerprint similarity, a miner analyzes the molecular graph itself to capture topology-based patterns.
